items.title: Ehizode: Canagerian for life, by Emeka Obasi
items.description: Welcome to Canada, the land where Nigeria’s first Commonwealth gold medal was achieved by Arinze Ifeajuna at Vancouver 1954. Daniel Igali won Olympic gold for the North Americans and also captained the team. Joe Ehizode, like many Nigerians, has found home in Surrey, British Columbia. He was a sports journalist before relocating nearly three decades ago. Denying his roots is out of it. What has come to stay is a middle way out, with malice towards none. He wrote : “I owe my undiluted allegiance to Canada first, and my country of birth Nigeria, second. But because Nigeria did not qualify for this World Cup, I found myself in a sea of match ups, swinging my support from one nation to another as the tournament progressed. It became a master class in modern identity.” I did not find this strange at all. Ehizode was my colleague at Champion House, Lagos. He could claim Esan or Igbo identity. His town of origin, Ekpon, is a border town between Edo and Delta States. Founded by Ijie who migrated from Ekpoma, the people are making the best of two worlds without dropping their Esan background. For now, what matters most is the Marple Leaf. And in defending Canada, Ehizode does not spare anyone who hurts his identity. When Mexico damaged South Africa, it was sweet music. “I could not bring myself to backing a nation whose recent History has been married by the Xenophobic actions of goons targeting fellow Africans,” he posited. America received the same treatment before the game with Paraguay. “I cannot in good conscience, support a country that habours political factions or rhetoric wanting to annex Canada. Absolutely not.” Donald Trump sure has got friends across the Northern border. Many Nigerians living in the United States and Canada are sad that the Super Eagles missed qualification. Femi Solaja lives in Vancouver, with his family. He did not travel to jump like Ifeajuna, who was nicknamed ‘Emma Vancouver.’ “It is really sad, considering the number of Nigerians in those countries. I stand to be corrected, Nigeria has the highest population of diaspora than other visiting teams to the World Cup. Nigeria got the vibes to make open watch party more entertaining. “Just like in the stadium as well. Sadly, all those who put us in this mess, are plotting their way back, first with the CAF Awards, before the election,” Femi told me. His elder brother, Kunle, is covering his tenth World Cup. Yemi Ojo lives in Baltimore, Maryland. As a Pastor, he prayed for the Eagles to land in America where they made their Mundial debut in 1994. There would have been an opportunity to send reports back home, like he did while active as a journalist. “It is very sad. The Eagles would have performed well in this World Cup See what Cabo Verde did to Argentina,” Ojo pointed out. It was also in the United States that Nigeria won Africa’s first Olympic soccer gold medal, in 1996. The Green Eagles were tipped to win a medal at the Montreal 1976 Games. Unfortunately, there was an African boycott because of apartheid South Africa. It is painful that the same blacks that received massive continental support have descended on their benefactors. Canada has been good to Ehizode and other Nigerians. In 1957, Onwura Zonyeuno (OZ) Chiazor, became the first African naval officer to be commissioned by Queen Elizabeth Ii. He was spotted by Dr. Dennis Osadebe who brought him home to join the Nigerian Navy. A second batch of Nigerian Air force cadets was sent o to Canada for training in 1963. In that group were August Okpe, Gibson Nwosu, Elendu Ukeje, Dan Suleiman, Danjuma Ato, Winston Aleyideino, George Musa Jebak and Gbadamosi King. From Cyprian Enweani to Rosey Ede, we have had Nigerians wearing Canadian colours in sports. Natalie Achonwa, Nayo Raincock – Ekunwe and Yvonne Ejim, are know names in basketball. Soccer boasts of Tani Oluwaseyi, Promise David, Fikayo Tomori and Simi Awujo. Ehizode remains a typical home boy. I have navigated the Ekpon, Ogwa, Ebelle, Opoji, Ewohimi, Igueben axis severally and know that Esan blood flows in their veins. When you see names like Emefiele, Chuks or Ijeoma Josephine Otabo, better known as Phyna of Big Brother Naija, remember they are rooted in Ekpon. As the World Cup was going on, Ehizode sent me a quick message – The Desk Must Bubble. That was our tattoo at Ilasamaja. It simply means let us make merry. He wired choice wine and turkey, all wrapped in Canadian dollars back home. A home boy in Surrey. Na so him be. “ I was born in Nigeria and that heritage is forever woven into my DNA. I have now spent half of my life in Canada. My family is here. I live, work and earn a living here. “Canada has given me a beautiful life. So, I am Canadian. My loyalty is to Canada first, and Nigeria second. I say this with absolute conviction and without apologies.” Bottom line: it is a win win draw. Mark the word, Canagerian. The post Ehizode: Canagerian for life, by Emeka Obasi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Is Gov Otti Tinubu’s agent? By Ugoji Egbujo
items.description: If every major ally of Peter Obi behaved exactly like Alex Otti, the practical effect would be a significantly weakened, fragmented, and less confrontational opposition ahead of 2027. And this isn’t because , he didnt move to the NDC with Peter Obi. No, far from it. This is because if all Obi’s allies adopted the same stance, the opposition would still exist, but it would look more like a collection of locally focused pragmatists than a disciplined alternative government-in-waiting. The moral and mobilising force of the Obidient project would be substantially diluted. Governor Hope Uzodinma declared that all Igbo governors were united in working for Tinubu’s re-election. Not that it matters. The people have often defied their governors at the polls. Yet Governor Otti quickly issued a disclaimer, insisting that Uzodinma, no matter how hopeful, could not speak for him. At a reception for Tinubu’s wife in Aba, however, Otti all but publicly endorsed the President with a deluge of superlatives. Is Otti’s disclaimer merely an otiose subterfuge? The elections are six months away. One function of a good leader is to offer the people authoritative direction with moral clarity at critical moments. Otti can no longer sit on the fence. There is no room for neutrality. His neutrality will amount to an endorsement of Tinubu’s continuation. If Tinubu has performed as outstandingly as Otti has proclaimed, then Otti should endorse him fully and stop playing hide-and-seek. He cannot run with the hare and hunt with the hound. If Otti is afraid of the consequences of criticising Tinubu, then he is neither a man of courage nor of conviction. The most committed Obidients thrive on moral clarity and a sense of existential struggle. When high-profile figures who rode the 2023 wave treat Tinubu with awe and admiration while focusing on state-level delivery, it becomes far harder to sustain the intensity, volunteer networks, and pressure that once characterised the movement. Many Obi supporters are not wrong to feel betrayed. Watching Otti showering ecomiums on Tinubu, the cause appears diluted, even abandoned, by some of its own beneficiaries. Otti must speak for himself. He says publicly that Tinubu has done well. Obi maintains that Tinubu has performed abysmally. Both cannot be correct. If Otti chooses to highlight a few of Tinubu’s good deeds while remaining silent on areas of atrocious performance, then, with respect to the 2027 elections, he is effectively a Tinubu promoter. In the coming contest he must make a clear choice and give objective reasons. That is leadership. I do not know how much gratitude Otti owes Obi, but he came to power partly on the back of Obi and the Obidients, even if he sometimes denies it. He remains in the Labour Party while Obi has moved to the NDC, but the general consensus among their supporters is that the two men belong to the same political family. That assumption now looks presumptuous in the face of Otti’s open political flirtation with Tinubu. The time for evasiveness and ambivalence is over. Otti cannot continue to support Tinubu by day and Obi by night. That is not tact; it is the behaviour of a chameleon. Otti has performed well as governor. He whispers to many that he needs Tinubu’s goodwill to attract projects and cooperation. His romance with the President is therefore presented as sheer pragmatism for the benefit of Abia. He knows that openly supporting Tinubu against Obi would pitch him against the Obidients, so he pretends to a tactful neutrality. Critics, however, call it convenient political promiscuity. That political atilogwu dance with Tinubu does nothing to advance Obi’s campaign, which Otti ought to champion boldly. Many argue it would be more honest for Otti to defect to the APC, as most other governors have done, than to remain in the opposition while blowing Tinubu’s trumpet and shining his shoes. However, it is instructive that the Obidients, who ordinarily run on a short fuse and a strong cancel culture, appear largely comfortable with the romance between Otti and Tinubu. Otti has neither been branded a traitor nor a sell-out. This is probably because he has performed so well that dissociating from him would cost political capital. In fact, Otti may be the only Igbo governor with the goodwill to deliver substantial votes for Tinubu in the South-East without resort to rigging. Yet if Otti is permitted to work for Tinubu from within the political shed of the Obidients, then the movement loses all moral authority to call out others who flirt with the President—including those who chose a clean divorce rather than quiet infidelity. It is disheartening to watch opposition governors lavish praise on a President who has failed to offer any morally transformative leadership. The danger of such capitulation is the steady slide toward one-party civilian autocracy. For democracy to thrive, the opposition must hold the ruling regime accountable. The notion that a governor must become a presidential shoe-shiner in order to secure cooperation or projects for his state is both ridiculous and corrosive. This philosophy of compulsory alignment with the centre has long been used by opposition governors who lack the courage for genuine opposition duties to excuse their own cowardice. Gov Alex Otti ‘s performance in Abia has been acknowledged. Nevertheless, he must be held accountable for every act of cowardice or moral confusion . The post Is Gov Otti Tinubu’s agent? By Ugoji Egbujo appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Trump’s Letter, Atiku’s Lobbyists and old American stories about Tinubu, by Emmanuel Aziken
items.description: Politics is often less about the event itself than about the timing of the event. A document released today may have been written weeks earlier, but when it surfaces at a politically sensitive moment, it immediately acquires a meaning far beyond its contents. That is the context in which the recent exchange involving President Bola Tinubu, former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and the administration of President Donald Trump should be understood. For weeks, reports had circulated that lobbyists engaged by Atiku were intensifying efforts in Washington to draw renewed attention to the decades-old American civil forfeiture case involving Tinubu. Whether those efforts ultimately succeed or not is almost secondary. Their immediate objective appears to be to keep alive a narrative that has trailed the President since before the 2023 election. Then, almost on cue, emerged a letter from President Trump commending the Tinubu administration’s efforts against insecurity and reaffirming the importance of Nigeria to American strategic interests. Coincidence? Perhaps. Calculated timing? That is the question political observers cannot ignore. This is not the first time Nigeria’s political class has sought advantage through Washington. Ahead of the 2015 presidential election, the then-opposition All Progressives Congress (APC) vigorously cultivated relationships within the Barack Obama administration and the wider American policy establishment. At the time, relations between Abuja and Washington had become strained over a number of issues, including the Jonathan administration’s handling of the Boko Haram insurgency and the enactment of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, which drew strong criticism from the Obama administration. Those developments fuelled a widespread perception in Nigerian political circles that Washington had become increasingly uncomfortable with President Goodluck Jonathan’s government. Whether that perception accurately reflected the position of the Obama White House is a matter historians may continue to debate. What is beyond dispute is that the APC recognised the importance of international opinion and invested considerable effort in engaging influential American policymakers and opinion moulders. It was a strategy aimed not necessarily at securing foreign intervention but at shaping the international narrative around Nigeria’s democratic transition. Many within the APC later believed those engagements contributed to strengthening global confidence in the credibility of the 2015 electoral process. It is, therefore, ironic that the same political tendency that once benefited from cultivating opinion in Washington now finds itself on the receiving end of a similar strategy. The actors have changed; the playbook has not. Within hours, the African Democratic Congress (ADC), now serving as the principal platform of the opposition coalition, dismissed the significance of the letter, insisting that commendation from Washington would not erase lingering questions surrounding the old forfeiture controversy. Expectedly, both sides are playing to their strengths. The Tinubu camp wants Nigerians and the international community to see a President who enjoys the confidence of the world’s most powerful government. International endorsements, especially from Washington, have always carried considerable political value in Nigeria. They reinforce the image of legitimacy and strengthen the government’s diplomatic standing. The opposition, however, sees something different. To it, no diplomatic nicety can substitute for accountability. In its calculation, the real issue remains the old American records which have refused to disappear from Nigeria’s political discourse. This is where the battle shifts from facts to perception. The Trump letter was never likely to persuade Tinubu’s critics. Equally, the lobbying campaign in Washington was never likely to shake the confidence of Tinubu’s supporters. Each development merely energises an audience that had already made up its mind. That explains why the ADC’s response came almost immediately. By declaring that “Trump’s letter cannot save Tinubu,” the opposition was sending a message not to Washington but to Nigerians. It was attempting to prevent the administration from converting diplomatic goodwill into domestic political capital. The Presidency, on its part, would undoubtedly relish every opportunity to project itself as a respected international partner at a time when Nigeria is seeking greater foreign investment, deeper security cooperation and stronger economic confidence. The larger question, however, is whether either strategy speaks to the concerns of ordinary Nigerians. The average citizen battling inflation, unemployment, insecurity and rising living costs is unlikely to lose sleep over lobbying contracts in Washington or congratulatory letters from foreign leaders. Those are elite political contests, fought with sophisticated public relations weapons thousands of kilometres away from the markets of Lagos, the farms of Agbor or the streets of Kano. For the ordinary Nigerian, performance remains the ultimate lobbyist. If insecurity declines substantially, investment improves and economic conditions become more bearable, international commendations will merely echo what citizens already feel. Conversely, if hardship persists, no number of endorsements from foreign capitals will significantly alter public opinion. Indeed, history teaches that external validation rarely determines domestic political fortunes. Nigerian voters have consistently judged leaders more by their personal experiences than by the opinions of foreign governments. Ultimately, neither Washington’s commendation nor Washington’s lobbying will decide Nigeria’s political future. That decision belongs to Nigerians. Letters may shape headlines. Lobbyists may shape conversations. Political parties may shape narratives. But elections are shaped by citizens assessing whether their lives have become safer, more prosperous and more hopeful. In the end, the most persuasive endorsement any government can receive is not a letter from a foreign president. It is the verdict of its own people. items.title: Towards healing a nation’s 60 yr old wound, by Muyiwa Adetiba
items.description: This is the sixtieth year – to the week – of the July 1966 coup that has been infamously regarded as a counter-coup. A coup thatunfortunately marked the degeneration of a Nigeria that our fore fathers strove for and tried to build.A coup that subsequently led to a thirty- month Civil War which still leaves a lingering bitter taste in many mouths today. It is called a counter-coup because there had been a coup six months earlier which turned out to be lopsided in its execution if not design. It has been argued severally, that this was not the plan but the grim reality turned out to be that this original coup wiped out a generation of Northern leaders and many South-western leaders in a gruesome and humiliating manner while sparing the counterpart leaders in the South-east. It also, perhaps inadvertently, upset the country’s delicate balance of power as people of South-eastern descent, subsequently occupied commanding heights across various sectors of the country. That this coup was largely led by young, indignant – some say ‘nationalistic’- Igbo Officers did not help matters. It was thereafter infamously labelled an Igbo Officers’ coup. The counter-coup could have been called a reprisal coup. Or a Northern Officers’ coup as it was powered by officers of Northern descent who had waited six months for a decisive action from their Commander-In- Chief – who happened to be Igbo – towards holding the executors of the January coup accountable for their actions. Instead, they were met with what seemed like vacillation and foot-dragging. Now, with the benefit of hindsight, neither of the two groups could have imagined the effect of these earliest of coups on the nation’s economic development, ethnic alignment and cultural cohesion. A friend recently sent me a report which stated that any country with a high Ethno-linguistic fractionalization (ELF), will never achieve its full potentials no matter highly endowed the country is. Broken down in plain English, it means a country that is not homogenous in language, religion, culture and ethos will never amount to much irrespective of its latent potentials. Nigeria has a high ELF. The task before our founding fathers was to see how to work with those differences to achieve a great nation. The potentials have always been there. But because of our high ELF, we are fully engaged in pulling ourselves in different directions because there is no common ethos, let alone a common goal. The two coups, tagged Igbo Officers’ and Northern Officers’ coups had exacerbated the fault lines. Even their constituency, the Military, which was the nation’s guiding light in inclusivity, fell prey to ethnicity and distrust. We are living the consequences of that today, sixty years after. Nations oftentimes learn from wars. Nationhood had been forged from experiences of civil wars in Europe and even in Africa where Rwanda comes to mind. But we seem to have learnt the wrong lessons in our dear Nigeria. Perhaps because there was, and still is, a lot of denial. A war was fought. And in every war, there are losses and casualties. These casualties are always more with the defeated. They could include property, land and sovereignty. In our case, there were winners and losers despite the rhetoric of the time. The slogan, ’No Victor, no Vanquished’ was to make reintegration easier. It was to make nation building faster. It was, in a way, to understate the fact that the victor of today could be the vanquished of tomorrow. Nothing after all in life is static. Unfortunately, many of our Igbo brethren came back focused on their losses. They came back with a heightened sense of victimhood. They came back more suspicious and distrusting. This has led to the profiling that ‘the Igbo don’t share well’. This is probably not true on an individual level because I know from personal experience that my Igbo friends are among the most generous. But as a collective, the Igbo seem more insular. And less tolerant of others ethnic groupings. This has led to a mutual distrust which plays out on the political stage.One side claims marginalization. The other side fears vengeance and exclusivity.A pointer is the sheer amount of venom poured out against Yoruba in the social media by people who live and earn their living in Yorubaland. Yet, it can be argued that the West has given more, in land, commerce and general opportunities, to the desired East-West collaboration than the East.An appreciation of host communities anywhere, will lead to more trust, less hostility and possibly less xenophobic reactions. We have to heal this 60 year-old wound even if we eventually break up due to our high ELF. It starts by acknowledging that no side is blameless in what Nigeria has become for all of us. Without the lopsidedness in the execution of the January coup, the tardiness or reluctance of the AguiyiIronsi’s governance to deal with the coupists, there might not have been a July coup.Without these two, and the reluctance of the then leaders – led by Gowon and Ojukwu – to compromise and make a deal, there might not have beena Civil War. It continues by recognizing that there were acts of humanity and compassion by ordinary folks before and during the war. There were folks, even in the north, who shielded their Igbo neighbors until they could safely travel. There were Igbo kids who were boarded and educated throughout the period in the South-west. There were properties and businesses that were preserved for their Igbo owners. Recognizing these small acts bring healing because they highlight our shared humanity. I read recently that there were moves by the Ironsi family to recognize the sacrificial act of Col AdekunleFajuyi who put his life on the line for his guest and Commander-In-Chief. That, if true, is a step in the right direction. To intentionally die for someone is the highest sacrifice that anybody can make and recognizing that fact is one way to go in healing the wounds of 1966. I believe, and may not be popular for saying this, that the Igbo have since gotten their place back and more from the commonwealth except the presidency. Even there, a positive move was made when Dr Alex Ekwueme, a nationalist if there was one, was elected Vice President as far back as 1979, and later when EmekaOjukwu was brought back from exile to the political arena. The rest is now left largely to the individual. Whoever wants to be President, or any form of national leadership, has to cultivate the trust of different nationalities that make up Nigeria. He has to address the prejudices that can affect his electoral success.It is ‘doable’. Simply playing the victim card is retrogressive and will not help. Neither will playing the emil’okan card. The post Towards healing a nation’s 60 yr old wound, by Muyiwa Adetiba appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: SEGUN ODEGBAMI: The 2026 World Cup – my take!
items.description: The 2026 FIFA World Cup has come and gone. My first take-away is the painful fact that Nigeria was absent. The pain lingers. That the Super Eagles were not a part of an event that gripped the attention of the whole world for a period of 6 weeks was a nightmare Nigerians must wake up from. The administration that failed the country must not return to power under any circumstance. Coaches are sacked, Players are dropped and Administrators voluntarily ‘retire’ or are shown the way out! Under no circumstances must the people that failed the country remain and sustain their unproductive, administrative prescription. Nigeria must not reward glaring failure. There must be No room for sentiments! In the midst of the excitement and entertainment of the matches during the World Cup, most other activities in the world receded to the background, giving way to the exhilarating drama of football matches that left humanity on the edge of their seats, night after night, for almost 6weeks. The power of football in the world was in full display. It confirms once again that sport is not just a powerful tool in the world, but has the power to change the world, for good. For 6 weeks, football brought all of humanity together (friends and enemies alike), uniting them in the ecstasy of wins (and losses) experienced in this highly unpredictable football game. People set aside their differences, hugging and kissing, fraternizing and ‘fighting’ without guns at venues spread around North America, celebrating friendship, peace and heroes of football. The past 6 weeks have been a long global ‘vacation’ for many people, even in the countries that did not have teams at the event. Everybody joined in the festival. Now, it has all ended. The 2026 World Cup may be the biggest single social event in history. More countries than ever before participated. More matches than ever were played. Attendance at the matches may be the highest in history. The media (particularly television) coverage was unprecedented. The broadcast was the most technologically sophisticated ever, with more eyes (cameras) covering every inch of grass on the field of play, and recording every action from every conceivable angle. Technology took over the ultimate decision-making on the field of play, even as some referees still demonstrated frailty in human judgment. Their inconsistency raised issues of bias, incompetency and powerful external influences. Africa’s representatives did very well. 9 out of the 10 crossed the Group stage into the round of 32 where all but two became separated from the ‘men’ that progressed to the round of 16. Most of the African teams put up great performances that showed clearly that the continent is fast closing up at the top hierarchy of world football. Losing in very close encounters against ‘giants’ was a clear indication and great advertisement. The domestic leagues were a determinant of progress. Countries with some of the best leagues eventually progressed to the latter stages of the competition, another clear indication that the championship is won not by accident but by consistent superior performance. The final match saw two teams with two traditions emerge – the best of South America and the best of Europe. In the end, deservedly, Europe won! Spain, the country with one of the biggest and best leagues and clubs in the world, hosting some of the best players on the planet, got to the finals. Argentina, with a huge football tradition, solid experience about how to win difficult matches at this level, and with the contributions of the greatest football player in history, Lionel Messi, playing an individual game unknown in the history of football, also worked their way to the final match. In the end, the better team won. Argentina had not played well throughout the championship. They won all their matches because of the same orthodox style the deployed, the presence of Messi and plenty of luck at the tail end of matches. Only God knows what would have happened even in the finals had the team not played the last quarter with one man less! All of that is history now. Spain has, deservedly, played their established ‘tiki taka’. The baton of individual greatness was handed to a new kid-on-the-block by the outgoing god – Lionel Messi. Lamin Yamal heralds a new beginning and a new star. At the same time, my revelation of the World Cup is a quiet ‘general’ in the heart of the Spanish team, a Libero, the man who orchestrated every move, controlled the pace and tempo of the midfield, transited elegantly from defense to attack, kept the ball jealousy, passed with super precision, and cut out Lionel Messi almost effortlessly and flawlessly. Rodri is the new King of football. The Manchester City FC playmaker makes the game look so simple, very elegant and absolutely beautiful. The Captain of Spain is my player of the 2026 World Cup! The post SEGUN ODEGBAMI: The 2026 World Cup – my take! appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Proposed AJ vs Itauma mega fight can surpass Rumble in the Jungle – Oboh
items.description: Balmoral Promotions is targeting a blockbuster heavyweight fight in Nigeria between Anthony Joshua and new heavyweight sensation, Moses Itauma for 2027 in Nigeria, though no official agreement is in place yet. The proposed bout is envisioned to happen in Lagos as a means of bringing home the two Anglo-British fighters whose roots are in Nigeria. This news has excited former Commonwealth and British light heavyweight boxing Champion Peter Idemudia Oboh, who, in his active days also fought under the British flag, the Union Jack. Reacting to the news, Oboh who has since returned to Nigeria said the history-making mega fight being put together by Dr Ezekiel Adamu, chief Executive Officer of Balmoral Promotions will be the first of its kind on Nigerian soil. “It will be historic and the bout will create a positive image for Nigeria.” The pugilist-turned pastor who was also the W.B.A International light heavyweight champion observed that “if such a fight will be possible, I would love to be involved in it because boxing can not be better or greater than such a mega show of two super fighters renowned exhibiting their skills for the first time in their father land.’ He continued, “these two boxing heroes are highly respected by boxing enthusiasts, including highly placed Nigerians. Such a fight can only be compared to the famous Mohammed Ali vs George Foreman Rumble in the Jungle fame that took place in Zaire in 1974. This fight will make history and maybe surpass the Mohammad Ali v George Forman 50-year fight and could go down as the biggest ever staged in the African continent.” He however, sees some obstacles which must be overcome if such a fight will ever hold. “I can see 5 major barriers that must be overcome for this super fight to happen and to stand any chance of happening in Nigeria. Moses Itauma and Anthony Joshua.” He mentioned the huge financial implications among other things. The post Proposed AJ vs Itauma mega fight can surpass Rumble in the Jungle – Oboh appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: NFF elective congress entangled in legal cobwebs
items.description: .A perpetration of illegality – Baribote .There’s no level playing field – Fuludu .September election already decided – Toro BY JACOB AJOM It is one week since the curtains fell on the 2026 FIFA World Cup in New York. Spain deservedly carted away the gold trophy at the expense of a conservative Argentina side. The better side won effortlessly as good football prevailed. For many Nigerians the outcome did not matter much, but the pain of not having been represented by the country’s flagship team, the Super Eagles has remained the sour point of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. A former chairman of the League Management Company, now NPFL, Rumson Victor Baribote said it was unthinkable that Nigeria, the giant of Africa, was absent out of ten countries that represented Africa at the Mundial..”It is something I don’t even want to think about. For a team that once ranked fifth in the whole world, it was embarrassing not to have qualified for the World Cup. It is a shame. It is not something that should be remembered or even thought about.” Baribote is not alone. Former Secretary General of the Nigeria Football Association(now NFF) Alhaji Sani Toro said, “It is unfortunate that we have failed to go to the World Cup in two consecutive editions. Our football has gone down and the government doesn’t seem to have the will to do anything about it.” A former Nigeria international, Edema Fuludu echoed, “Every Nigerian football fan is still bitter that in two consecutive World Cups we did not attend. It shows that we need to do more, apart from just talking. We must work on the talk.” Working the talk, Fuludu insisted, means “the NFF must not go the former round where we just talk about going back to the drawing board when we don’t have a drawing board. Nigeria has to be in the next World Cup.” That means things must change. How does the change come about when the people who are resisting change are still in charge of affairs? Corroborating Fuludu’s fears, Baribote said, “ If we were in a saner clime, those who are at the helm of affairs should have humbly stepped aside honourably and relinquished their positions, but not here.” The bigger worry is that the Nigeria Football Federation has fixed September 26 for its elective congress which will produce a new executive. Almost all members of the present board want to return and campaigns are already in high gear. The campaign slogan of the NFF President Ibrahim Gusau is ‘continuity’ Toro said nothing will change as the September election has already been concluded. “This coming election is already concluded,” he told this writer. “They will only remove one or two people who do not agree with them. So don’t expect any change at the end of the election. The same people will come back.” Asked if he was interested in the forthcoming election, Fukudu laughed it off. “Only a fool will throw his hat into the ring for a fight he knows he cannot win,” he said. “There is no level playing field,” he remarked, adding, “It’s good to be ambitious, but there is no level playing field. Under which platform will I be coming from? You must come from a platform which can give you some votes. Now there is a lot of inequality(imbalance) in the way votes are being given at NFF elections. That is what the players’ Union has been fighting. Let us have a level playing field so that knowledgeable people can willingly go to contest. As it is now, someone like Okocha or Odegbami can only get one vote if they want to contest. For instance, if I am coming from a state FA there is no way I can contest for the Presidency against the incumbent because he is on top of the FAs; where they have 36 votes plus. If I am coming from the players Union I will have only one vote, a coach has only one vote. So where is the fairness in it? That is the problem; no level playing ground. So it is not as if one doesn’t want to be ambitious. There is no fairness in the whole thing. Unless you are a fool, you can’t just throw your hat into the ring because you won’t get the vote required to win”. Baribote assured that something can still be done to correct the imbalance in the voting pattern before the September election. He argued that the real actors who make football possible were being relegated in the running of their own affairs by those he termed as ‘outsiders’. “If you look at a football match,” he began, “who are those that are the real actors on the pitch? The players, the referees and the coaches and here they don’t have the opportunity to manage their own affairs, while those that are not active are the people calling the shots. That is why we are having this problem.” He continued, “out of 44 voting rights, the FAs get 36, with FCT it becomes 37. So, how can one unit produce a president at the expense of the other four? And even the League chairmen that are supposed to be elected, are appointed into office by the NFF board. “Now the NFF just pick whoever they like and impose him on the clubs as League chairman, Who elected him? I was chairman of the league at the time, I was elected by the clubs.” Baribote said FIFA recognizes that clubs elect or appoint their own person, not somebody coming to interfere. So, there’s a lot of illegality going on. “Even in the Nigerian constitution, for you to be president, you must have at least two thirds of votes in a number of states. But in the Nigerian Football Federation, it’s only one unit, which is the state FAs, that elect instead of the collective mandate of all the stakeholders.” Justifying his objection to the status quo, Baribote said, “Now, let me give you one simple analogy. For you to be a referee in Nigeria, to officiate games, you must have passed through training or a test of the Nigerian Referee Association, to qualify as an NRA member. To be a coach, you must have the minimum qualification of the NIS as a coach and to be a member of the players’ union, you must have played professionally. That is the qualification. Now tell me what qualifies the FA Chairmen? Nothing.” Fuludu said, the fight to correct the imbalance has been on for long. “Even the Players Union led by Harrison Jalla had to go to court but some of us in the union decided not to go the same route and avoid the courts by talking to some stakeholders and people in the National Sports Commission. The so-called amendments made at the Extraordinary Assembly in Bayelsa were cosmetic. If anything, it shows that they still don’t want to provide a level-playing field. There is no verifiable change.” We asked if it has become a helpless case? His answer was blunt. “It appears so, unless the government steps in and says, ‘enough of this. Let us have a comprehensive list and let no one threaten us with FIFA, so that people with real interest and good intentions for Nigeria football will come out to contest. Once they are assured of a level playing field, the best candidates will come out to contest”. Toro who supervised one of the most successful eras of Nigerian football said the situation can only be rectified by the government. The NFF Statutes that appear so lopsided can be amended to reflect fairness and equal representation of stakeholders if the government stands firm. “It is easy to deal with and nobody should threaten us with FIFA sanctions. Unfortunately, the government has not demonstrated enough will to effect the desired change. The chairman of the National Sports Commission, Shehu Dikko said there will be changes but I think only a miracle can bring about this change.” Baribote declared that the present board of NFF cannot be talking about another election when the election that brought them to power had been declared illegal by the Appeal Court. Said he, “We shouldn’t be talking about whether they should come back because their being in office alone is illegal. There is a standing order given by the Court of Appeal dated 19th January, 2024 that nullified their election. They filed an appeal and the Court of Appeal on the 29th of September, 2022 gave an interim order when they looked at the propriety of their appeal and on January 19th, 2024, struck out their appeal and further directed the deletion of that appeal number from the court of appeal. Yet they are in office. We have filed contempt proceedings, we have filed for the enforcement of that order. They are still in office. So, you see that there is no legal mandate putting them in office because the election that put them there, in the first place, is still being challenged in the court of Appeal and they want to go ahead with another election because they have no respect for judicial pronouncements and the rule of law. Like I said, one day a Moses will come that will take us to the Promise Land. So, we are on it, we are not going back. So, ordinarily, in the eyes of the law, they are not even known because their being in office is illegal.” The post NFF elective congress entangled in legal cobwebs appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Les caniveaux ne votent pas, mais ils parlent
items.description: © Internet À chaque hivernage, Bamako reçoit le même avertissement. Les rues se remplissent d’eau, des habitations sont envahies et les dégâts relancent le débat sur l’assainissement. La pluie déclenche la crise, mais elle n’en explique pas à elle seule l’ampleur. Les réseaux de drainage insuffisants, les collecteurs mal entretenus et les constructions érigées dans certains passages naturels de l’eau relèvent de la responsabilité publique. Mais il existe aussi une responsabilité plus proche, plus quotidienne et souvent plus difficile à reconnaître. Celle du citoyen qui transforme le caniveau en poubelle. Un sachet jeté dans la rue paraît insignifiant. Ajouté à des milliers d’autres, il finit pourtant par ralentir l’écoulement, obstruer un passage et aggraver les conséquences d’une forte pluie. Salir aujourd’hui et réclamer demain une ville propre constitue une contradiction que l’on ne peut plus ignorer. Aucun État, aussi efficace soit-il, ne peut construire une ville contre ses propres habitants. Les autorités doivent construire des ouvrages adaptés, assurer la collecte des ordures, curer régulièrement les caniveaux et sanctionner les dépôts anarchiques. Mais aucune politique d’assainissement ne peut produire des résultats durables si les ouvrages nettoyés sont aussitôt remplis de déchets. La responsabilité commence aussi devant les maisons, dans les marchés, le long des rues et autour des dépôts improvisés. La pluie est un phénomène naturel. Les infrastructures défaillantes relèvent de l’action publique. Jeter ses ordures dans un caniveau est un choix individuel. Les inondations naissent souvent de la rencontre de ces trois réalités. Les prévenir suppose donc moins de désignation et davantage de responsabilités partagées. Salimata Wagué

items.title: Prince Owusu completes four-year move to DAC 1904
items.description: Slovak top-flight side DAC 1904 have completed the signing of Ghanaian forward Prince Owusu from Azerbaijani club Gabala SC on a four-year contract. The highly-rated youngster joins the Slovak outfit after beginning his professional career at Gabala, where he signed his first professional contract following his rise through the ranks of Nayan Soccer Academy in Ghana. Owusu spent several years at the Accra-based academy, establishing himself as one of its brightest prospects. He played a key role in helping the club secure promotion to the Greater Accra Regional Football Association (GARFA) Division Two League during the 2024/25 season. The striker was also prolific in the Ga North Division Three League, scoring 25 goals and providing 16 assists in 30 appearances, earning a reputation as one of the most exciting young forwards in Ghana’s lower-tier football. EXCL: Slovak top-flight side DAC 1904 have reached an agreement to sign Prince Owusu from Gabala SC. The highly-rated Ghanaian forward landed in Austria a few hours ago to undergo his medical ahead of completing the move. Owusu, a product of Nayan Soccer Academy, has also… pic.twitter.com/8NmYz4MaJY — Joseph Ayinga-Walter (@AyingaWalter) July 24, 2026 His performances were rewarded with call-ups to Ghana’s U19 and U20 national teams, further highlighting his potential. After moving to Azerbaijan to join Gabala, Owusu continued his development in European football before attracting interest from DAC 1904. The Slovak club have now secured his services on a four-year contract, with the move representing another important milestone in the young forward’s career. Owusu will be aiming to establish himself in the Niké Liga as he continues his development and seeks to fulfil his potential in European football.

items.title: Commonwealth Games: Can Ajayi end Nigeria’s 96 years jinx in men’s 100m in Glasgow?
items.description: By Douglas Baye-Osagie Athletics historians can’t wait for a better opportunity than now to believe Nigeria is on the verge of winning one of the most elusive gold medals in our sports history. Despite a rich avalanche of great sprinters, a men’s 100m gold medal at the Commonwealth Games has been embarrassingly elusive. For 96 years, the Commonwealth Games have rolled around like clockwork. The gun first cracked in Hamilton 1930, the steel city of Canada. Then it echoed in London 1934, and through the Commonwealth in cities like Sydney, Auckland, Cardiff, Kingston, Edinburgh, Kuala Lumpur, Manchester, Brisbane, Victoria, Delhi, and Birmingham 2022. Now, the circuit returns once again to Glasgow 2026, and with it, Nigeria’s 96-year wait for a men’s 100m crown. Our women have already left their mark with pride. Mary Onyali gave us fire and fight, winning 100m gold in Victoria 1994. Blessing Okagbare gave us grace and dominance, winning 100m gold in Glasgow 2014 and setting the Commonwealth Games record at 10.85s on that same track. Tobi Amusan continued the tradition in the last edition, taking 100m hurdles gold in Birmingham 2022 and setting a Games record of 12.30s. The green and white has danced on the podium in the sprints before. The Nigerian women have answered the call. And we’ve proven it can be done in para sports too. Nigeria already holds a Commonwealth 100m mark, just not in the able-bodied category. Adekunle Adesoji stormed to gold and set the para sports 100m record of 10.76s in Manchester 2002. It was a reminder that speed runs in our DNA. That a Nigerian can go to the Commonwealth Games, face the world, and leave with the fastest time. If we could do it in para athletics, why not in the marquee men’s 100m? But the men’s 100m? That has been our ghost story. It wasn’t always this way on the track. Some men have tried and pushed for the ultimate prize, but it never came home. Nigeria first announced herself as a sprinting giant in the relays. Christchurch 1974 — Benedict Majekodunmi, James Olakunle, Kola Abdulai, Timon Oyebami won bronze in the 4x100m in 39.70s. Our first men’s sprint medal at the Games and at international level. Eight years later, Brisbane 1982 — Lawrence Adegbehingbe, Iziaq Adeyanju, Ikpoto Eseme, Samson Oyeledun took it further and won GOLD in 39.15s, beating a Canadian team with the great Ben Johnson (the fastest man in the 1980s and the first to break the 9.90 and 9.80 seconds barriers). That was the statement. Nigeria had sprinters. Nigeria could run. Nigeria could win. The world took notice. But somehow, the magic never translated to the individual 100m – the stage where just one man is the leader and pride of the pack. The 1990s once gave us hope, as it was a decade of fantastic sprinters. Auckland 1990 was supposed to be the breakthrough. For the first and only time in Commonwealth history, Nigeria put three men into the same 100m final — Davidson Ezinwa, Osmond Ezinwa, and Abdullahi Tetengi. The country buzzed. Finally, we would have our man on the podium. But the dream died on the line at Mount Smart Stadium in January 1990. Ezinwa finished 4th in 10.26s. Osmond was 6th. Tetengi 8th. Gold went to Linford Christie of Great Britain. The green and white left empty-handed again. That Auckland final remains Nigeria’s biggest showing in the event. It heralded hope, but also began a pattern: close, but not close enough. After 1990, it would be 12 years before another Nigerian — Uchenna Emedolu — won silver in 2002. Then Fasuba took silver again in 2006. Since then, only Enoch Adegoke made the final in 2018, finishing 7th. Despite producing some of Africa’s fastest men — Davidson Ezinwa who ran 9.94, Chidi Imoh, Seun Ogunkoya, Olusoji Fasuba who held the African record at 9.85, Deji Aliu with his Olympic bronze pedigree — no Nigerian man has ever stood atop that Commonwealth 100m podium. Not in 22 editions. Not once. We’ve been at the arena, smelt it, but never tasted victory. It is the one gap in an otherwise proud sprinting CV. This is not the Olympics where the Americans hold sway, it is the Commonwealth Games. The Yorubas will say Kilode! What is our problem? And in Glasgow 2026, that gap may finally close. Waiting in the blocks now is Kanyinsola Ajayi. As we say in local parlance, “our hope don rise, eyes dey shook.” The expectations are palpable and the National Sports Commission is already rehearsing its victory dance in anticipation of history. The boy from Oreyo, Ikorodu, is no longer running to escape schoolwork like he did in Secondary School in Lagos. He is running to make history. At 21, Ajayi has already done things Nigerian sprinting has begged for. He stands toe-toe with the world’s best and, after making an Olympic semi-final in Paris 2024, he has been a phenomenon on the track. He has broken Olusoji Fasuba’s 20-year-old 100m national record of 9.85s with a time of 9.84s. From Ikorodu to the world. He even beat an Olympic champion on the biggest stage. And he may not stop at just winning gold in Glasgow. The Commonwealth Games 100m record has stood at 9.88 seconds since 1998, set by Trinidad and Tobago’s Ato Boldon in Kuala Lumpur. It is a mark that has survived 7 editions of the Games. Konyinsola Ajayi is entering the Games in hot form, and with the wind at his back, even Boldon’s 28-year-old record could be under serious threat. With Ajayi already clocking 9.84s in London, pundits believe the Nigerian has both the gold and the record in his sights. “He can win it and rewrite the books.” The timing feels poetic. Glasgow, the city where Okagbare won gold and set the record in 2014, will host again in 2026. Nigeria, the nation that has watched others take our event, now has a genuine contender who can take both the title and the record. From the 1974 relay bronze team, to the 1982 gold team, to Ezinwa, to Fasuba, to Aliu — the baton has been passed. The women have delivered gold and records. Now it rests with a kid from Ikorodu who grew up watching them on TV. At the 2026 London Athletics Meet, held on 18 July at London Stadium — the eleventh leg of the Diamond League for the year — Konyinsola Ajayi didn’t just run. He announced himself with a legendary finish. The United States-based sprinter stood tall among giants and produced another statement — 9.84 seconds to win it. He outpaced reigning world champion Oblique Seville of Jamaica, 9.87s, while home favourite Romell Glave of Great Britain chased in a personal best of 9.97s. In one race, Ajayi turned hope into belief. He showed he can win outside Africa, win when the critics are watching, win against world champions and win when the lights are brightest. For Nigerian sports enthusiasts, that 9.84 was more than a time. It was a promise. Eyes that had waited 96 years suddenly fixed themselves on Glasgow, daring to dream of an elusive crown in our nation’s sports history. After that blistering race, Ajayi now carries something else: the hunger of a nation that has waited 96 years. Could this be the year Nigeria stops waiting, breaks the jinx … and starts winning? In Glasgow, at Scotstoun Stadium, the gun will crack again. And for the first time in a very long time, Nigeria may just be the one crossing the line first — possibly with a new Games record to boot, from the boy Konyinsola Ajayi who grew up in Ikorodu. The post Commonwealth Games: Can Ajayi end Nigeria’s 96 years jinx in men’s 100m in Glasgow? appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Trump cites ‘white, male, Christian’ audit in Smithsonian disclaimer push
items.description: US President Donald Trump has issued an executive order to install signage that warns visitors of inaccurate historical information inside the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History in Washington. The highly unusual move marks the 80-year-old Republican’s latest battle in his ideological war on American cultural institutions and monuments, some of which he has renamed for himself and renovated to his liking despite legal challenges. The order issued on Friday calls on federal...

items.title: Trump’s Trigger Warnings
items.description: Incensed by the Smithsonian but lacking immediate power to do anything about it, Donald Trump has resorted to trolling the world’s largest museum complex from the sidewalk. In an executive order posted this afternoon, the president directed the Department of the Interior to place signs outside the National Museum of American History warning passersby about “ideological capture” and detailing the findings of his administration’s recent, quickly contested report on the museum. The order comes days after the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, was grilled by lawmakers on Capitol Hill. The warnings, the order says, will direct visitors to “locations and resources for accurate information” about American history and will notify them that exhibits “should be renovated consistent with the findings of the Report.” It asserts that the “current leadership of both the Smithsonian Institution and the Museum cannot be trusted to tell America’s story with honesty and gratitude.” Having determined, perhaps, that the museum’s 250-object exhibit “exploring the ideals of the Declaration of Independence” is not enough, Trump also ordered the Department of the Interior to mount its own temporary exhibits outside that will “appropriately honor the 56 signers” of the document. To the White House, the order is probably meant to escalate its public-pressure campaign on the Smithsonian, which began with an executive order last spring calling to rid the institution of “improper ideology” and restore it “to its rightful place as a symbol of inspiration and American greatness.” In short, Trump feels that the museums are too negative about the country’s history and should be more patriotic, and the Smithsonian argues that its museums can be celebratory and present complex stories at the same time. Instead, the call to place trigger warnings outside the museum reflects the limitations of the Trump administration’s power in this instance, as well as a weakness in its campaign to seize control of the American story. The Smithsonian occupies a strange place as a public-private partnership and “independent federal trust instrumentality” of the U.S. government. Partially funded by the federal government, the institution is governed by a board of regents, which does not have presidential appointees and can’t be purged in the way that the board of the Kennedy Center was . Although in some specific cases the Smithsonian has been treated as part of the executive branch and in others it has not, the institution is not an executive agency and not overseen by the president like the National Park Service is (NPS is managed by the Interior Department). That means the Smithsonian is also not susceptible to the type of mandated history scrubbing that NPS leadership has enforced at historic sites across the country. Trump is directing Interior Secretary Doug Burgum in this new order because he cannot officially direct Hartig, and neither can he direct Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch, who reports to the board of regents. The signs will go on the NPS-controlled sidewalks and walkways because that’s where the White House can have a say. The White House looks to even be aware of these limitations in the executive order, urging the heads of the Interior Department, the Office of Management and Budget, and the General Services Administration, as well as the assistant to the president for domestic policy to “identify and utilize any and all available authorities to promote the policy of this order.” This includes “any mechanisms available to encourage correction of the issues identified in the Report.” The naming of the OMB appears to nod to previous threats that the White House has made about hinging the Smithsonian’s apportioned funds on its compliance with Trump’s vision, which likely would be illegal. In its July 4 report on the American-history museum, the White House argued, essentially, that the museum has been politicized and that it “no longer treats the American story as a shared national inheritance to be taught or celebrated, but as a political instrument to divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens.” It criticizes what it calls “anti-White” advocacy and takes specific aim at museum representations of transgender Americans and undocumented immigrants, as well as exhibits featuring Filipino and Mexican Americans, describing as activism what many might simply see as mentions of people who exist in this country. The report repeatedly calls out museum staffers by name, and Hartig appears in more than a dozen images throughout the document. Speaking in one of the congressional hearings this week, Representative Melanie Stansbury, a New Mexico Democrat, called it “a political witch hunt.” During those dizzying hearings, Hartig tried to defend her and her colleagues’ work. She told lawmakers that the museum is nonpartisan, and that it uses “historical evidence” and “competing perspectives” and acknowledges “enduring debates.” She said that the museum’s goal is to “preserve and document the evidence of American life in all of its breadth, so that the public can encounter the past and draw their own conclusions,” and that telling the full story of history “is a form of respect for the American people.” None of this, of course, stopped the accusations of activism or a GOP witness and even one lawmaker from calling for a cleaning-out of the institution’s leadership. The hearing was theater. The signs are too. A kind of turf war has taken place across the National Mall this summer. The Great American State Fair , the signs plastered with Trump’s slogan “We are making D.C. Safe and Beautiful,” and the ever troubled Reflecting Pool —the president’s hand has been ubiquitous in America’s backyard. Still, these incoming signs will mark a new kind of outward hostility, falling somewhere closer to putting Trump’s name on the Kennedy Center. To publicly take aim at a beloved American institution could risk doing exactly what Trump accuses the Smithsonian of in the report: dividing. But there’s something that the president, it seems, has not considered. Trump and his coterie love to talk about “freedom-loving” Americans, and those freedom-loving Americans don’t exactly love being told what to do. Some of them might even see these signs outside the museum and have all the more reason to walk right on in.

items.title: Protection sociale : les journalistes face au défi de l’affiliation
items.description: © JDM Réunis le 24 juillet 2026 au Mémorial Modibo Keïta de Bamako, professionnels des médias, pouvoirs publics et organismes sociaux ont examiné les obstacles à la couverture sociale des journalistes. La rencontre intervient dans un secteur où la précarité contractuelle prive encore une grande partie des travailleurs de l’assurance maladie, des prestations familiales et de la retraite. L’Union des journalistes reporters du Mali (UJRM) a organisé, vendredi 24 juillet 2026, une journée de réflexion sur la protection sociale des professionnels des médias. Tenue en prélude à la cinquième édition de la Nuit de l’UJRM, la rencontre avait pour thème « Journalisme et précarité : entre devoir et déboires ». Elle a bénéficié de l’appui de la Fondation Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung. Les échanges se sont appuyés sur une réalité déjà documentée par l’organisation. Une enquête menée par l’UJRM en 2025 auprès de 200 journalistes à Bamako et dans huit autres localités indiquait que 63 % des répondants ne disposaient pas d’un contrat de travail formel. Elle établissait également que 74,5 % ne bénéficiaient d’aucune couverture sociale et que la moitié travaillait sans rémunération stable. La journée a porté sur les dispositions du Code du travail, le Code de prévoyance sociale, les démarches d’affiliation et les difficultés rencontrées par les entreprises de presse pour déclarer régulièrement leurs employés. Le cadre légal impose pourtant à l’employeur de s’affilier au régime de prévoyance sociale et de faire immatriculer ses salariés. La rencontre a réuni notamment Bandiougou Danté, président de la Maison de la presse, Mohamed Ag Albachar, chef de cabinet du ministre de la Communication, de l’Économie numérique et de la Modernisation de l’Administration, ainsi que des représentants de l’Institut national de prévoyance sociale. Les travaux ont été modérés par le journaliste Salif Sanogo. Dans sa présentation, Sékou Issa Diarra, inspecteur de sécurité sociale à l’INPS, a détaillé les prestations auxquelles l’affiliation peut ouvrir droit. Elles concernent notamment les risques professionnels, les prestations familiales et la retraite. Il a insisté sur la régularité des déclarations et des cotisations, indispensable au maintien effectif des droits des travailleurs. Pour le président de l’UJRM, Boubacar Kanouté, la question ne se limite pas aux revenus. Elle touche aussi à la stabilité professionnelle et à la capacité du journaliste à faire face à la maladie, à un accident ou à la fin de sa carrière. « Un journaliste qui exerce sans couverture en cas de maladie, d’accident professionnel ou sans garantie pour son avenir reste exposé à une grande vulnérabilité », a-t-il déclaré. Mohamed Ag Albachar a présenté la protection sociale comme une condition nécessaire à l’exercice d’une presse professionnelle et responsable. Il a reconnu que les difficultés économiques des médias freinent encore la formalisation de nombreux emplois et appelé à une action associant les pouvoirs publics, les employeurs, les organisations professionnelles et les partenaires. Le représentant de la Fondation Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung a également insisté sur la responsabilité partagée des différents acteurs. Les discussions ont principalement porté sur la formalisation des contrats de travail, l’affiliation effective des journalistes et le versement régulier des cotisations sociales. Joseph Amara Dembélé

items.title: Secrétariat général de l’ONU : Macky Sall dévoile sa feuille de route !
items.description: Quelques jours après avoir obtenu le soutien officiel du Sénégal à sa candidature au poste de Secrétaire général des Nations unies, l'ancien président Macky Sall accélère sa campagne diplomatique. Dans une déclaration rendue publique jeudi, il a présenté les grandes priorités qui guideraient ses premiers jours de mandat s'il était élu à la tête de l'organisation. L'ancien chef de l'État sénégalais affirme vouloir agir rapidement afin de « restaurer la confiance » au sein des Nations unies. Une priorité qu'il considère indispensable dans un contexte marqué par la multiplication des conflits, les tensions géopolitiques, les crises climatiques et les difficultés de financement auxquelles fait face l'institution. Selon lui, les premiers jours d'un mandat doivent envoyer un signal fort. Son programme prévoit notamment une consultation des différentes composantes du système onusien, une évaluation des réformes en cours ainsi que l'ouverture de discussions avec les États membres afin d'améliorer l'efficacité et la crédibilité de l'organisation. Cette prise de parole intervient dans un contexte politique particulier. Lundi dernier, le président Bassirou Diomaye Faye a officiellement annoncé que le Sénégal soutenait la candidature de son prédécesseur, qualifiant cette ambition de candidature portée au service du Sénégal, de l'Afrique et du multilatéralisme. Macky Sall avait salué cette décision, y voyant un geste d'unité nationale au-delà des divergences politiques. En choisissant de détailler son agenda dès les premiers jours d'un éventuel mandat, Macky Sall cherche également à se distinguer des autres candidats en présentant une vision concrète plutôt qu'un simple programme de principes. Cette démarche s'inscrit dans une campagne où la capacité à proposer des réformes crédibles sera déterminante auprès des États membres appelés à désigner le successeur d'António Guterres. Toutefois, cette candidature continue de susciter des réactions contrastées au Sénégal. Si elle bénéficie désormais du soutien officiel de l'État, plusieurs organisations de victimes des violences politiques des années 2021-2024 continuent d'exprimer leur opposition, estimant que les procédures judiciaires doivent suivre leur cours avant toute consécration internationale. En présentant une feuille de route centrée sur la restauration de la confiance, l'efficacité administrative et la réforme du multilatéralisme, Macky Sall poursuit désormais une campagne résolument tournée vers la scène internationale, où chaque prise de parole vise à convaincre les États membres de sa capacité à conduire les Nations unies dans un environnement mondial particulièrement instable.

items.title: Tanger : levée du Pavillon Bleu à Tanja Marina Bay et sur trois plages atlantiques
items.description: Le Pavillon Bleu a été levé au port de plaisance Tanja Marina Bay, ainsi que sur les plages Achakar, Sol et Ba Kacem, situées sur la façade atlantique de la ville de Tanger. Cette distinction environnementale, attribuée par la Fondation Mohammed VI pour la protection de l’environnement (FM6E), a été hissée lors d’une cérémonie organisée à cette occasion, en présence du secrétaire général de la wilaya de la région Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceima, du président du Conseil communal de Tanger, de représentants de la Fondation, ainsi que de plusieurs acteurs institutionnels concernés. L’obtention de ce label reflète les efforts déployés par la commune de Tanger et la société gestionnaire du port « Tanja Marina Bay » pour répondre aux critères établis par la FM6E, présidée par Lalla Hasnaa. Ces critères portent notamment sur la qualité des eaux de baignade, l’information et la sensibilisation, l’éducation à l’environnement, ainsi que les aspects liés à la santé, la sécurité, l’aménagement et la gestion. Dans une déclaration à la presse, le président du Conseil communal de Tanger, Mounir Laymouri, a souligné que certaines de ces plages ont conservé le Pavillon Bleu pour la 13ème année consécutive, témoignant des efforts continus déployés pour préserver la propreté et la qualité des eaux conformément aux normes environnementales internationales, en plus des services d’animation et de loisirs offerts. « Nous sommes fiers que la ville de Tanger ait réussi à maintenir ce label pour quatre sites balnéaires et de loisirs cette année, et nous aspirons à en augmenter le nombre l’année prochaine », a-t-il ajouté. Par ailleurs, le Pavillon Bleu flotte pour la troisième année consécutive au port de plaisance « Tanja Marina Bay », consacrant ainsi l’engagement constant de cette infrastructure en faveur de la protection de l’environnement et de la biodiversité. Dans un communiqué de presse, la société Tanja Marina Bay International a indiqué que cette distinction conforte la position du port en tant que « référence du tourisme nautique responsable au Maroc et à l’échelle régionale ». A noter que dans le cadre du respect des exigences de ce label, le port de plaisance Tanja Marina Bay a mis en place un dispositif renforcé de gestion environnementale, comprenant notamment la collecte sélective des déchets, la récupération des huiles usagées et des eaux de cale, le suivi régulier de la qualité des eaux et la prévention de la pollution, ainsi que l’organisation d’activités de sensibilisation au profit des plaisanciers, des usagers et du grand public pour la préservation du littoral. The post Tanger : levée du Pavillon Bleu à Tanja Marina Bay et sur trois plages atlantiques appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Religion : « La foi doit unir les hommes, ne jamais les diviser », indique le Cheikh Tang Zoug Moré
items.description: Dans un Burkina Faso confronté à l'insécurité et aux fractures sociales, certains leaders religieux choisissent de répondre aux défis par le dialogue plutôt que par les discours de division. Parmi eux, Redwane Pougda, connu sous le nom de Cheikh Tang Zoug Moré, fait de la religion un levier de paix, de solidarité et de rapprochement entre les communautés. Guide religieux, enseignant, président d'une association engagée pour la cohésion sociale, chantre de louanges islamiques et commerçant, il défend la conviction selon laquelle la foi n'a de sens que lorsqu'elle rapproche les hommes. Serein, le regard posé et le sourire discret, Cheikh Tang Zoug Moré inspire davantage par son attitude que par de grands effets de manche. Ceux qui le côtoient décrivent un homme accessible, attentif aux autres et profondément attaché au dialogue. Son engagement ne se limite pas à la mosquée. Il accompagne les familles, conseille les jeunes, soutient les personnes vulnérables et multiplie les initiatives en faveur du vivre-ensemble. ‎« La foi représente ma vie », résume-t-il simplement. Originaire de Yourga, dans l'est du Burkina Faso, Redwane Pougda découvre très jeune sa vocation religieuse. En 2006, la visite d'un maître venu enseigner l'islam dans son village bouleverse son destin. Avec l'accord de son père, il quitte l'école classique pour se consacrer entièrement à l'apprentissage des sciences islamiques. Son parcours de formation le conduit à Nakiboane, dans la région de Fada N'Gourma, puis à Bobo-Dioulasso, avant de poursuivre ses études en Égypte, au Niger et au Ghana. Ces années passées à l'étranger lui permettent d'approfondir sa maîtrise de la langue arabe, des sciences religieuses et de l'enseignement islamique. ‎À son retour au Burkina Faso, il reprend progressivement le flambeau de son grand-père, lui-même guide religieux. Aujourd'hui, il forme de nombreux élèves qui, à leur tour, transmettent les enseignements reçus. Mais pour lui, enseigner la religion ne consiste pas uniquement à apprendre des versets ou des règles. Il s'agit surtout d'éduquer des citoyens capables de vivre avec les autres. « Les différences religieuses ne doivent jamais devenir des motifs de conflit, mais des occasions de mieux se connaître », affirme-t-il. ‎Cette vision guide chacune de ses interventions. Dans ses prêches comme dans ses rencontres avec les populations, il insiste sur la responsabilité de chacun dans la préservation de la paix. ‎Pour Cheikh Tang Zoug Moré, aucune religion authentique ne peut appeler à la haine. La foi doit conduire au respect, à l'humilité et à la solidarité. « Le jugement appartient uniquement à Dieu », rappelle-t-il régulièrement. À ses yeux, le croyant ne peut prétendre aimer Dieu tout en rejetant son prochain. « Même si une personne n'a pas la même vision que moi, elle reste un être humain. Je lui dois de l'empathie, de l'amour et du respect. Qu'elle soit musulmane ou non, il faut l'accepter et la respecter. » ‎Son message dépasse ainsi largement les frontières confessionnelles. Il défend une société où musulmans, chrétiens et adeptes des religions traditionnelles peuvent vivre ensemble dans le respect mutuel. Cette approche prend tout son sens dans le contexte actuel du Burkina Faso. « La religion est importante, mais elle n'a pas de sens en dehors d'un territoire. C'est le pays qui doit primer sur nos actions », explique-t-il. Pour illustrer cette idée, il évoque souvent un épisode de la vie du prophète Mohammed. « Le jour où le Prophète a quitté La Mecque a été l'un des plus douloureux de sa vie. Cela montre combien l'attachement à sa terre est essentiel. Nous devons tout faire pour préserver notre pays et renforcer la cohésion sociale. » ‎Au-delà de ses enseignements religieux, Cheikh Tang Zoug Moré agit concrètement à travers une association officiellement reconnue depuis 2025. Celle-ci mène des campagnes de sensibilisation à la paix, encourage le dialogue interreligieux, accompagne les personnes vulnérables, développe des actions de solidarité, encadre les jeunes et promeut les valeurs citoyennes. ‎« Concernant nos actions, nous faisons les choses dans la mesure de nos capacités. Les leaders religieux sont nombreux et nous collaborons lorsque cela est nécessaire. Nous sommes des frères d'une même famille dans l'islam et dans le Burkina tout entier », explique-t-il. Selon le Cheikh Tang Zoug Moré, la foi doit être au service de la paix, du dialogue et de la cohésion sociale ‎Selon lui, chaque leader religieux, coutumier ou social a sa part de responsabilité dans la construction d'une société plus apaisée. « Pour faire grandir la communauté, il faut être droit et prêcher une parole juste qui unit les gens au lieu de les diviser. » ‎Son parcours personnel n'a pourtant pas été exempt d'épreuves. Alors qu'il poursuit ses études religieuses au Ghana, il perd tous ses moyens de subsistance. Isolé, sans ressources et loin des siens, il passe plusieurs jours sous un pont, survivant grâce aux restes de nourriture récupérés auprès des restaurants. ‎Cette période difficile prend fin lorsque les forces de l'ordre parviennent à contacter sa famille installée à Cinkansé. ‎Loin de nourrir de l'amertume, cette expérience renforce sa foi et sa détermination. Elle lui apprend que la persévérance et la confiance en Dieu permettent de traverser les moments les plus éprouvants, affirme-t-il. ‎Aujourd'hui encore, cette épreuve nourrit son engagement auprès des plus démunis. Pour lui, la véritable pratique religieuse se mesure dans les actes quotidiens. « La véritable foi se mesure à travers les actes de solidarité, de respect et d'amour envers les autres », insiste-t-il. ‎Dans chacun de ses engagements, Cheikh Tang Zoug Moré indique poursuivre l'objectif de contribuer, à son échelle, à bâtir un Burkina Faso où les différences deviennent une richesse plutôt qu'un facteur de division. Et à travers ses enseignements, ses actions sociales et sa proximité avec les populations, il rappelle qu'au-delà des appartenances religieuses, la paix reste une responsabilité collective. Une responsabilité qui commence par un regard bienveillant sur l'autre et par la conviction que la foi trouve sa plus belle expression lorsqu'elle sert l'humain, précise le Cheikh. ‎ ‎Farida Thiombiano ‎Lefaso.net ‎

items.description: El incendio que afecta al suroeste de la Comunidad de Madrid alcanzó durante la tarde de este viernes su “momento álgido” y varios de sus frentes están “fuera de capacidad de extinción”, según el consejero de Medio Ambiente, Carlos Novillo. Los tres frentes que afectaban a la región ya se han fusionado en uno único, que ha obligado a evacuar Chapinería, Navas del Rey, Colmenar del Arroyo, Fresnedillas de la Oliva, Robledo de Chavela, Aldea del Fresno, Navalagamella y Zarzalejo, mientras San Martín de Valdeiglesias, Pelayos de la Presa y Villa del Prado permanecen confinados. El Ministerio del Interior ha elevado a 63.000 el total de evacuados o confinados entre Madrid y Ávila, tras sumarse un camping de 5.000 personas en El Escorial, hacia donde se dirige ahora el fuego. “La gran misión” es proteger ese municipio y San Lorenzo de El Escorial, para lo que la UME trabaja en una línea de defensa. La superficie quemada podría rondar ya las 12.000 hectáreas, casi el doble que al mediodía, y no se han comunicado daños personales. En Ávila, la Subdelegación del Gobierno ha ampliado el confinamiento a Cebreros y Navaluenga y ha ordenado evacuar Hoyo de Pinares, Burgohondo y Villanueva de Ávila.
